description: This 3 mile walk takes you from Arthog to Barmouth using the Cross Britain Way and the Wales Coast Path. Walk Report October 14th 2026 By David Hughes: We parked at the car park near Arthog Hall and set off towards Barmouth, with the Mawddach Estuary providing the backdrop for what turned out to be a really enjoyable walk. It was one of those places where I found myself stopping every few minutes, not because I was tired, but because the views kept changing and there was always something else to look at. The estuary is broad and open here, with the hills of southern Snowdonia rising around the water and the coastline opening out towards the sea.The highlight was crossing Barmouth Bridge, the long wooden railway bridge that carries both the railway and a pedestrian walkway across the mouth of the estuary. It feels quite different from crossing an ordinary road bridge. You’re right above the water, with boats and mudflats below and the mountains stretching away inland. I spent a good while looking back towards Arthog and along the estuary towards the mountains. The views are especially rewarding when the tide is out and the channels of water wind through the exposed sand and mud. Keep an eye out for birds feeding along the shoreline too, as the estuary is an important habitat for wading birds and other wildlife.Although the bridge is the main attraction, I enjoyed the contrast between the quieter surroundings at Arthog and the livelier atmosphere on the Barmouth side. The bridge is also part of the famous Mawddach Trail, a largely level walking and cycling route that follows a former railway line beside the estuary between Barmouth and Dolgellau. It’s easy to see why the area is so popular with walkers and cyclists, with so much scenery to enjoy without needing to climb high into the mountains.Once across the bridge, we continued into Barmouth and made our way towards the seafront. The change of scene was lovely: from the open estuary and mountain views to the wide sandy beach, promenade and colourful seaside town. Barmouth has a traditional holiday atmosphere, with cafés, independent shops and places to stop for an ice cream after the walk. We finished by the sea, where it was good to sit for a while and watch the waves coming in. On a clear day, the views along the coast are excellent, and the beach gives you plenty of room to stretch out and enjoy the fresh air.This is a walk where I’d recommend taking your time rather than rushing straight across the bridge. The estuary scenery is the real reward, and the bridge itself is an experience as well as a useful crossing. Do check the weather before setting off, as the exposed bridge can feel breezy, and take care around the railway crossing points. Finishing on Barmouth’s seafront makes it a satisfying one-way walk, with plenty of options for refreshments before heading home.
